1.title: Storage
1.text: Welcome to Module 7: Storage. This module is in the Container Orchestration domain, and it covers the topic called Storage. By the end you will be able to do four things. Compare ephemeral and persistent storage, and the common volume types. Explain Persistent Volumes, claims and binding. Use Storage Classes, access modes and reclaim policies in a scenario. And describe C S I, expansion, snapshots and Stateful Set storage.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Keeps Its Data
1.text: At Harbor Books, the postgres database holds every order, so its data must survive when its Pod is replaced or moves to another node. The cache only needs scratch space that can disappear with its Pod. And the platform team wants storage to be created on demand, not by hand for each request. In this module you give each part the right kind of storage.

1.title: Volumes: Ephemeral and Persistent
1.text: Start with how long data must live. A container's own filesystem is ephemeral. After a crash, the kube let restarts the container with a clean state. A volume is a directory that the containers of a Pod can use and share. Ephemeral volumes are created and deleted with the Pod. Persistent volumes have a lifecycle independent of any Pod, so the data stays when the Pod moves. The diagram shows three bars of growing length: the container filesystem, an empty Dir, and a Persistent Volume. Exam tip: ask how long the data must live. The container, the Pod, or longer.

1.title: Common Volume Types
1.text: Six volume types to know. An empty Dir starts empty once the Pod has been given a node. Its containers share it. It is deleted with the Pod, but it is safe across container crashes. A host Path mounts a file or directory from the node's filesystem. It has many security risks, so avoid it. A local volume is a disk, partition or directory on a node, used as a static Persistent Volume. Config Map and secret volumes fill files from a Config Map or a Secret. A projected volume maps several sources into one directory, all from the Pod's namespace. And a persistent Volume Claim is the way a Pod uses a Persistent Volume. Exam tip: an empty Dir lives and dies with its Pod. Avoid host Path.

1.title: PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim
1.text: A Persistent Volume, or P V, is storage that the cluster offers, with a lifecycle independent of any Pod. A Persistent Volume Claim, or P V C, is a user's request for storage, with a size and access modes. A control loop binds each claim to a matching P V, one to one. And if no P V matches, the claim stays unbound until one appears. In the diagram, the Pod uses the claim by name. The claim is bound to a volume. And the volume is backed by real storage, such as a disk, N F S or a cloud volume. The application team writes the Pod and the claim. Exam tip: Pods use claims, and claims bind volumes.

1.title: Using a Claim
1.text: Here is a claim for the postgres data. It asks for a size, here five gibibytes, access modes, here Read Write Once, and optionally a Storage Class. A Pod uses the claim with persistent Volume Claim and a claim name in its volumes. The claim and the Pod must share a namespace. And a claim that a Pod is using is protected from immediate removal. Exam tip: the Pod names the claim, in its own namespace.

1.title: StorageClass and Dynamic Provisioning
1.text: A Storage Class describes a class of storage, with a provisioner, parameters and a reclaim policy. Dynamic provisioning creates a volume on demand when a claim asks for it, so nobody pre-creates Persistent Volumes by hand. A claim with no storage Class name gets the default Storage Class. In the diagram, the claim names a class, the provisioner creates the volume, and the new P V is bound to the claim. The binding mode matters too. Wait For First Consumer waits until a Pod uses the claim, so the volume matches where the Pod runs. The default mode is Immediate. Exam tip: claim in, Storage Class decides, P V out.

1.title: Access Modes and Reclaim Policy
1.text: There are four access modes. Read Write Once, R W O, is read-write by a single node. Read Only Many, R O X, is read-only by many nodes. Read Write Many, R W X, is read-write by many nodes. And Read Write Once Pod, R W O P, is read-write by a single Pod in the whole cluster. Then the reclaim policy. With Retain, when the claim is deleted, the P V is Released and keeps its data until an administrator reclaims it. With Delete, the volume is deleted with the claim, and a dynamically provisioned volume follows its Storage Class, which defaults to Delete. Recycle is deprecated. Exam tip: R W O is per node, R W O P is per Pod, Retain keeps data, and Delete removes it.

1.title: CSI, Expansion and Snapshots
1.text: C S I, the Container Storage Interface, is a standard interface for exposing storage systems to containers. A vendor ships a driver that is built outside the Kubernetes code base, unlike the older in-tree plugins. In the diagram, Kubernetes talks to the C S I driver, and the driver talks to the storage system. Expansion works by editing the P V C to ask for more storage, if its Storage Class sets allow Volume Expansion. And snapshots work through a Volume Snapshot, which requests a snapshot of a volume. It is a C R D, and it needs a C S I driver. Exam tip: C S I is the standard plug-in interface for storage drivers.

1.title: StatefulSet Storage and Storage Types
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. A Stateful Set uses volume Claim Templates to give each replica its own claim. Those claims stay when the Pods or the Stateful Set go away. You remove them by hand, unless a retention policy says otherwise. For storage types, file storage is a filesystem mounted into a directory, which is the default volume mode. Block storage is a raw device with no filesystem, and the application must handle it. Rook, a C N C F graduated project, orchestrates Ceph, which offers file, block and object storage. Exam tip: a Stateful Set's claims outlive its Pods.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: To recap. Data lives in the container filesystem, in an empty Dir as long as the Pod, or in a Persistent Volume beyond the Pod. A P V C requests storage, a control loop binds it to one P V, and the Pod names the claim in its own namespace. A Storage Class has a provisioner, parameters and a reclaim policy, dynamic provisioning creates volumes on demand, and the default class fills in for a claim with no class. R W O is per node and R W O P is per Pod, and Retain keeps data while Delete removes it. C S I is the standard driver interface, with expansion and snapshots. And a Stateful Set has one claim per replica, kept when Pods go. Now six practice questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A container in a Pod with an empty Dir volume crashes and is restarted. Later the Pod is removed from its node. What happens to the files in the empty Dir? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. An empty Dir is created once the Pod has a node. A crashing container does not remove the Pod, so the data survives the restart, but it is deleted permanently when the Pod is removed from the node.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. The Harbor Books postgres Pod must keep its data when it is replaced and started on another node. Which object does the team create to ask for that storage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A claim requests persistent storage, and the Pod uses it by name, so the data stays when the Pod moves. An empty Dir is deleted with the Pod, a host Path ties the data to one node, and a Persistent Volume is not owned by a Pod.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A Persistent Volume Claim names no storage Class name, and the cluster has a default Storage Class. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A claim with no class gets the default Storage Class, and dynamic provisioning then creates a matching volume on demand. Nobody has to pre-create a P V, and binding always matches size and access modes.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which access mode lets only one Pod in the whole cluster mount a volume read-write? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Read Write Once Pod allows read-write use by a single Pod across the whole cluster. Read Write Once is per node, so several Pods on that node can still use the volume.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Harbor Books deletes the claim of a test database, and the reclaim policy of the bound Persistent Volume is Retain. What happens to the volume and its data? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Retain allows manual reclamation. The P V is Released and keeps its data. Delete would remove the volume, and Recycle, the basic scrub, is deprecated.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. What does the Container Storage Interface, C S I, make possible? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. C S I is a standard interface between Kubernetes and storage systems, and drivers live outside the Kubernetes code base. It has nothing to do with node networking, image builds or scheduling.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, B: an empty Dir survives a crash and is deleted with the Pod. Question two, D: a Persistent Volume Claim, used by name. Question three, A: the default Storage Class provisions a volume. Question four, C: Read Write Once Pod means a single Pod. Question five, B: Retain keeps the volume and its data. Question six, A: C S I lets vendors add drivers outside Kubernetes.
